content: Maple trees, scientifically classified under the genus Acer (pronounced /ˈeɪsər/), are a group of trees or shrubs commonly referred to as maples. These plants are taxonomically categorized either in their own family, Aceraceae, or grouped with the Hippocastanaceae within the family Sapindaceae. Modern botanical classification systems, such as the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group system, favor their inclusion in the Sapindaceae family. The type species of the genus Acer is Acer pseudoplatanus, commonly known as the sycamore maple. There are approximately 128 recognized species of maples, most of which are native to Asia. However, several species are also found in Europe, northern Africa, and North America. Only one species, Acer laurinum, which has been poorly studied, is native to the Southern Hemisphere. Of the known maple species, 54 are classified as threatened with extinction in their natural habitats according to the criteria established by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). The genus name Acer is derived from the Latin word meaning sharp, a reference to the pointed tips characteristic of maple leaves. This name was first applied to the genus by the French botanist Joseph Pitton de Tournefort in the year 1700. The earliest known fossil evidence of a maple species is Acer alaskense, which dates back to the Late Paleocene epoch and was discovered in Alaska.
